items.prompt: What is a client-side cache, in the context of this unit?
choices: A local copy of data already fetched from the server, reused on a later request instead of fetching again
A place on the server where user passwords are stored
A browser setting that blocks all network requests
A backup of the entire application's source code
items.explanation: A cache remembers what was already fetched so a later request for the same data can reuse it instead of re-asking the server for something that hasn't changed.
items.reference:
💾 Cache — remembers a prior response
♻️ Reuse — skip a redundant network request

Why: re-fetching data you already have is wasted work — a cache is the fix for that specific waste, not for slow writes.

items.prompt: Why does revisiting a page that fetches the same data over and over waste effort, even if each individual fetch succeeds?
choices: Because each fetch re-requests data that likely hasn't changed since the last fetch, when a cached copy could have been reused instead
Because fetching data is always a bug regardless of context
Because browsers only allow a limited number of total fetches per session
Because servers charge extra for repeated identical requests
items.explanation: If the underlying data hasn't changed, re-fetching it is redundant work — a cache lets the page reuse what it already retrieved instead of asking again.
items.reference:
💾 Cache — remembers a prior response
♻️ Reuse — skip a redundant network request

Why: re-fetching data you already have is wasted work — a cache is the fix for that specific waste, not for slow writes.

items.prompt: What does "cache invalidation" mean?
choices: Deleting the entire cache permanently and never caching again
Marking cached data as no longer trustworthy, so the next read fetches fresh data instead of serving the stale copy
A server-side setting that disables all caching
Encrypting cached data for security
items.explanation: Invalidation marks a specific cached entry as stale because the underlying data changed, so the next read goes to the server instead of serving outdated cached data.
items.reference:
🚫 Invalidation — mark cached data as no longer trustworthy
🔄 Next read — fetches fresh instead of reusing stale data

Why: caching without invalidation eventually serves data that's known to be wrong — invalidation is what keeps a cache honest.

items.prompt: What's the risk of a cache that is never invalidated after the underlying data changes?
choices: None — a cache always stays accurate on its own
It will keep serving outdated data indefinitely, actively misleading the UI instead of just being redundant
The application will crash immediately
The cache will automatically empty itself after one use
items.explanation: Without invalidation, a cache has no way to know its data is outdated — it will keep serving the stale copy forever, which is worse than simply being redundant.
items.reference:
🚫 Invalidation — mark cached data as no longer trustworthy
🔄 Next read — fetches fresh instead of reusing stale data

Why: caching without invalidation eventually serves data that's known to be wrong — invalidation is what keeps a cache honest.

items.prompt: What does "stale-while-revalidate" mean?
choices: Blocking the UI until fresh data arrives, every single time
Showing the cached (possibly outdated) data immediately, while a fresh request runs in the background to update it
Deleting old data as soon as it becomes outdated
Refusing to show any data older than one second
items.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate shows the cached data right away for an instant response, then quietly checks the server in the background and updates the UI if the fresh response differs.
items.reference:
⚡ Instant — show cached data immediately
🔍 Background — re-check the server, update if different

Why: this trades a moment of possible staleness for never showing a blank/loading screen when a cached answer already exists.

items.prompt: In stale-while-revalidate, what happens if the background re-fetch finds the data actually changed?
choices: Nothing — the UI keeps showing the original cached version forever
The cache is updated and the UI is updated to reflect the fresh data
The application throws an error and stops working
The user is logged out automatically
items.explanation: If the background fetch's result differs from what was cached, the cache is updated and the UI reflects the corrected data — the user briefly saw stale data, then it self-corrected.
items.reference:
⚡ Instant — show cached data immediately
🔍 Background — re-check the server, update if different

Why: this trades a moment of possible staleness for never showing a blank/loading screen when a cached answer already exists.

items.prompt: What is an "optimistic update"?
choices: Updating the UI immediately as if a write request already succeeded, without waiting for the server's response first
A server setting that always approves every write request
Waiting for two separate server confirmations before updating the UI
A type of database backup
items.explanation: An optimistic update shows the assumed post-write result immediately, before the server has actually confirmed it — the UI reflects the user's intent right away instead of waiting on the round trip.
items.reference:
☑️ Click — UI updates immediately
📡 Server confirms — separately, in the background

Why: the user's intent is known the instant they click — an optimistic update reflects that immediately instead of waiting for confirmation.

items.prompt: Why does an optimistic update make a checkbox feel faster, even though the server still takes the same 800ms to respond?
choices: Because it actually makes the network faster
Because the UI shows the result of the click immediately, instead of waiting for the 800ms server round trip before showing anything
Because it skips sending the request to the server entirely
Because it caches the server's response before the click happens
items.explanation: The network timing doesn't change — what changes is when the UI shows the result relative to when the server confirms it. The UI no longer waits on the round trip to reflect the click.
items.reference:
☑️ Click — UI updates immediately
📡 Server confirms — separately, in the background

Why: the user's intent is known the instant they click — an optimistic update reflects that immediately instead of waiting for confirmation.

items.prompt: What is a "rollback" in the context of an optimistic update?
choices: Undoing an optimistic update and restoring the previous UI state, used when the server's actual response is a failure
Restarting the entire application from scratch
A server-side log of every request ever made
Automatically retrying a failed request forever
items.explanation: A rollback restores the UI to its state from before the optimistic change, used specifically when the server later reports that the write actually failed or was rejected.
items.reference:
📸 Snapshot — remember the exact prior state
↩️ Rollback — restore it if the server says no

Why: an optimistic update assumes success — a rollback is what happens when that assumption turns out to be wrong.

items.prompt: Why does an optimistic update need a rollback path, not just the initial immediate UI update?
choices: Because without it, a failed write leaves the UI showing a false state that was never actually true
Because rollbacks make the initial update happen faster
Because servers require rollbacks by law
Rollbacks are optional and rarely needed in practice
items.explanation: If the server rejects the write and nothing rolls back the optimistic change, the UI keeps showing a state that never actually happened — actively misleading, not just delayed.
items.reference:
📸 Snapshot — remember the exact prior state
↩️ Rollback — restore it if the server says no

Why: an optimistic update assumes success — a rollback is what happens when that assumption turns out to be wrong.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, why does the checkbox stay visibly unchecked for 800ms after the user clicks it?
choices: Because the click handler has a bug
Because the UI waits for the server's confirmation before showing the checked state at all
Because the network is completely disconnected
Because the checkbox is disabled by default
items.explanation: The naive version doesn't show anything until the server responds — the 800ms the user experiences is the full round trip, not a bug in the click handling itself.
items.reference:
☑️ Click — user checks off "Buy milk"
⏳ Wait — 800ms round trip to the server
✅ Then — checkmark finally appears

Why: the delay is real network time — the fix isn't making the network faster, it's not waiting on it to show the click's result.

items.prompt: Some users click the checkbox a second time during the 800ms delay in the opening scenario. Why?
choices: Because they think the first click didn't register, since nothing visibly changed yet
Because double-clicking is required to check off a task
Because the app instructs them to click twice
Because the checkbox is intentionally hard to click
items.explanation: With no immediate visual feedback, users reasonably assume their first click failed and click again — this is a direct, observable cost of the naive wait-for-confirmation approach.
items.reference:
☑️ Click — user checks off "Buy milk"
⏳ Wait — 800ms round trip to the server
✅ Then — checkmark finally appears

Why: the delay is real network time — the fix isn't making the network faster, it's not waiting on it to show the click's result.

items.prompt: This unit says re-fetching unchanged data and waiting on a slow write are "two different problems." What's the key difference between them?
choices: One is about reading data (GET), the other is about writing data (PATCH/POST/DELETE) — they need different fixes
There is no real difference — both are fixed by adding more servers
One only happens on mobile devices
One is a browser bug, the other is a server bug
items.explanation: Re-fetching unchanged data is a reading problem, solved by caching. Waiting on a slow write is a writing problem, solved by optimistic updates — they look similar ("the UI feels slow") but need opposite-direction fixes.
items.reference:
CachingOptimistic updates
DirectionReading (GET)Writing (PATCH/POST)

Why: conflating these two leads to trying to "cache" a write, or trying to make a read "optimistic" — neither maps onto the actual mechanism.

items.prompt: L2's sequence diagrams show the naive and optimistic versions both taking exactly 800ms for the server to respond. What actually changed between the two versions?
choices: The network became faster in the optimistic version
When the UI shows the result of the click, relative to when the server confirms it — not the network timing itself
The optimistic version skips sending the request to the server
The server processes the optimistic version's request differently
items.explanation: Both diagrams show an identical 800ms server round trip — the only difference is that the optimistic version shows the checked state immediately instead of waiting for the server to confirm it first.
items.reference:
🐢 Naive — UI updates only after 800ms confirmation
⚡ Optimistic — UI updates immediately, confirmation catches up after

Why: the server timing is identical in both — this is purely about when the UI decides to reflect the result.

items.prompt: Why is it accurate to say the optimistic update version is "honest" rather than just faster?
choices: Because it reflects the user's already-known intent immediately, rather than delaying the display of something that's already decided
Because it never sends a request to the server at all
Because the server responds faster when optimistic updates are used
Because it always shows the correct final state with no possibility of being wrong
items.explanation: The user's intent (checking the box) is known the instant they click — showing that immediately isn't a trick, it's reflecting information the UI already has, while the confirmation catches up separately.
items.reference:
🐢 Naive — UI updates only after 800ms confirmation
⚡ Optimistic — UI updates immediately, confirmation catches up after

Why: the server timing is identical in both — this is purely about when the UI decides to reflect the result.

items.prompt: In L2's stale-while-revalidate flowchart, what happens if the cached response is available AND the background re-fetch finds no difference?
choices: The UI shows the cached data instantly, and nothing visibly changes after the background re-fetch completes
The UI shows a loading spinner the entire time
The cached data is deleted immediately
The page automatically reloads
items.explanation: When the cache is available, it's shown instantly. If the background revalidation confirms nothing changed, there's no visible update needed — the cached data was already correct.
items.reference:
✅ Cached + unchanged — instant show, no visible update needed
🔄 Cached + changed — instant show, then corrected
🐢 No cache — must wait, show loading state

Why: the flowchart's three branches cover every combination of "is there a cache" and "did the background check find a difference."

items.prompt: In L2's stale-while-revalidate flowchart, what happens when there's no cached response at all?
choices: The UI must fetch and show a loading state — there's nothing to show instantly yet
The UI shows an error message immediately
The request is silently dropped
The UI shows cached data from a completely different page
items.explanation: Without a cached response, there's no stale data to show while waiting — the UI has to fetch fresh and show a loading state until that first response arrives.
items.reference:
✅ Cached + unchanged — instant show, no visible update needed
🔄 Cached + changed — instant show, then corrected
🐢 No cache — must wait, show loading state

Why: the flowchart's three branches cover every combination of "is there a cache" and "did the background check find a difference."

items.prompt: L2 lists three pieces a correct optimistic update needs. What are they?
choices: Snapshot the prior state, apply the optimistic change, and on failure restore the snapshot and surface the failure
Send the request, wait for a response, then update the UI
Cache the response, invalidate it, then re-fetch
Apply the change, log it, and never check for failure
items.explanation: All three steps matter: without a snapshot there's nothing exact to restore; without surfacing the failure, a silent rollback hides that anything went wrong from the caller.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Snapshot — the exact prior state
2️⃣ Apply — the optimistic change, immediately
3️⃣ On failure — restore + surface the error

Why: skipping any one of these three either loses the ability to roll back precisely, or hides a real failure from the rest of the app.

items.prompt: Why does simply reloading the page NOT count as "handling" a failed optimistic update, per L2?
choices: Because it only corrects the UI the next time the user happens to reload — until then, the UI keeps showing a false state
Because reloading the page is technically impossible in modern browsers
Because reloading always causes data loss
Because reloading is slower than the original 800ms wait
items.explanation: Relying on an eventual reload to fix a bad optimistic state means the UI shows an actively false state for an indefinite period in between — a deliberate rollback path is what closes that gap immediately.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Snapshot — the exact prior state
2️⃣ Apply — the optimistic change, immediately
3️⃣ On failure — restore + surface the error

Why: skipping any one of these three either loses the ability to roll back precisely, or hides a real failure from the rest of the app.

items.prompt: L2 warns that stale-while-revalidate is the wrong choice for some kinds of data. What's an example, and why?
choices: A live account balance or real-time price — even a few seconds of staleness could be unacceptable there
A list of blog post titles that rarely change — staleness there is fine
A user's saved theme preference — staleness there is fine
Static help documentation — staleness there is fine
items.explanation: Stale-while-revalidate always shows possibly-outdated data first — for data where even brief staleness is unacceptable, like a live balance, that trade-off is the wrong one to make.
items.reference:
✅ Good fit — data where brief staleness is harmless
❌ Bad fit — live balances, real-time prices, anything time-sensitive

Why: stale-while-revalidate is a deliberate trade-off, not a universal default — it has to match how much staleness the data can tolerate.

items.prompt: Why is it inaccurate to say stale-while-revalidate means "the user never sees stale data"?
choices: It means the user sees stale data briefly and gets corrected automatically — not that staleness never happens
Stale-while-revalidate never actually caches anything
The user always sees an error instead of stale data
Stale data is impossible once caching is implemented
items.explanation: The whole mechanism relies on showing the (possibly stale) cached value first, then correcting it — staleness is part of the design, not something the pattern eliminates.
items.reference:
✅ Good fit — data where brief staleness is harmless
❌ Bad fit — live balances, real-time prices, anything time-sensitive

Why: stale-while-revalidate is a deliberate trade-off, not a universal default — it has to match how much staleness the data can tolerate.

items.prompt: L2's comparison table lists a different "risk if wrong" for caching versus optimistic updates. What's the risk specific to caching?
choices: The cached data is stale — it no longer matches what the server actually has
The server crashes whenever a cache exists
The user's write request gets sent twice
There is no risk at all with caching
items.explanation: Caching's risk is serving data that's now out of date relative to the server — this is exactly what invalidation and stale-while-revalidate exist to manage.
items.reference:
CachingOptimistic
Risk if wrongStale dataNeeds rollback

Why: each technique fails in a different way when its assumption breaks — matching the failure mode to the mechanism makes both easier to reason about.

items.prompt: L2's comparison table lists a different "risk if wrong" for caching versus optimistic updates. What's the risk specific to optimistic updates?
choices: The optimistic state has to be rolled back if the server's actual response disagrees
The browser cache fills up and crashes the tab
The network becomes permanently disconnected
There is no risk at all with optimistic updates
items.explanation: Optimistic updates assume success before it's confirmed — the risk is specifically that the assumption is wrong and the shown state has to be undone via rollback.
items.reference:
CachingOptimistic
Risk if wrongStale dataNeeds rollback

Why: each technique fails in a different way when its assumption breaks — matching the failure mode to the mechanism makes both easier to reason about.

items.prompt: In L2's optimistic sequence diagram, what happens visually at the moment the server's 200 OK response actually arrives?
choices: Nothing visible changes, because the UI already showed the checked state — the response just confirms what was already assumed
The checkbox becomes checked for the first time
The page reloads automatically
An error message appears
items.explanation: By the time the server confirms, the UI already reflects the checked state from the optimistic update — the confirmation arriving is a non-event visually, since nothing needs to change.
items.reference:
⚡ Click — checkbox shows checked instantly
📡 800ms later — server confirms, nothing visibly changes

Why: this is the entire point of the optimistic pattern — the confirmation matters for correctness, not for what the user sees.

items.prompt: Comparing L2's two sequence diagrams, at what point does the naive version's UI first show the checked state?
choices: Only after the server's 200 OK response arrives, 800ms after the click
Immediately when the user clicks
Before the user even clicks
It never shows the checked state in the naive version
items.explanation: The naive diagram shows the UI waiting through the full 800ms round trip before updating — the checked state only appears once the server's confirmation is received.
items.reference:
⚡ Click — checkbox shows checked instantly
📡 800ms later — server confirms, nothing visibly changes

Why: this is the entire point of the optimistic pattern — the confirmation matters for correctness, not for what the user sees.

items.prompt: Implement `fetchTasksCached(cache, key, fetcher, onUpdate)`. `cache` has `.get(key)` and `.set(key, value)`. If `cache.get(key)` returns a value, return it immediately, but also call `fetcher()` in the background — if the resolved value differs (by `JSON.stringify` comparison) from what was cached, update the cache and call `onUpdate(freshValue)`. If nothing is cached yet, `await fetcher()`, store the result in the cache, and return it.

tests.description: first call with no cache awaits the fetcher and stores the result
tests.expr: (() => { const store = new Map(); const cache = { get: (k) => store.get(k), set: (k, v) => store.set(k, v) }; let count = 0; const fetcher = async () => { count++; return { id: 1 }; }; return fetchTasksCached(cache, 'k', fetcher, () => {}).then((r) => { expect(count).toBe(1); return expect(r).toEqual({ id: 1 }); }); })()

tests.description: second call with a cache hit returns the cached value immediately without awaiting the fetcher
tests.expr: (() => { const store = new Map([['k', { id: 1 }]]); const cache = { get: (k) => store.get(k), set: (k, v) => store.set(k, v) }; const fetcher = async () => { await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 50)); return { id: 2 }; }; return fetchTasksCached(cache, 'k', fetcher, () => {}).then((r) => expect(r).toEqual({ id: 1 })); })()

tests.description: onUpdate fires with fresh data when the background fetch differs from the cache
tests.expr: (() => { const store = new Map([['k', { id: 1 }]]); const cache = { get: (k) => store.get(k), set: (k, v) => store.set(k, v) }; const fetcher = async () => ({ id: 2 }); let updated = null; return fetchTasksCached(cache, 'k', fetcher, (fresh) => { updated = fresh; }).then(() => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(() => { expect(updated).toEqual({ id: 2 }); resolve(); }, 20))); })()

tests.description: onUpdate does not fire when the background fetch matches the cache
tests.expr: (() => { const store = new Map([['k', { id: 1 }]]); const cache = { get: (k) => store.get(k), set: (k, v) => store.set(k, v) }; const fetcher = async () => ({ id: 1 }); let updated = null; return fetchTasksCached(cache, 'k', fetcher, (fresh) => { updated = fresh; }).then(() => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(() => { expect(updated).toBe(null); resolve(); }, 20))); })()

items.explanation: On a cache hit, the cached value is returned right away while fetcher() runs in the background — comparing its result to the cached value decides whether onUpdate fires. On a cache miss, there's nothing to show yet, so the function awaits fetcher() before returning. This is exactly L3's fetchTasksCached, node-verified against a changing and an unchanged background response.
items.reference:
⚡ Cache hit — return instantly, check in background
🐢 Cache miss — await the network, then cache + return

Why: this is L3's exact stale-while-revalidate implementation — the same one node-verified against a changing background response.

items.prompt: Implement `toggleTaskOptimistic({ tasks, taskId, patchFn, onOptimisticUpdate, onRollback })`. Find the task with `id === taskId`, build a new array with that task's `done` flipped, call `onOptimisticUpdate(newArray)` immediately, then call `patchFn(taskId, { done: <new value> })`. If it resolves, return the optimistic array. If it rejects, call `onRollback(tasks)` with the ORIGINAL array (not the optimistic one) and re-throw the error.

tests.description: calls onOptimisticUpdate immediately with the flipped value
tests.expr: (() => { const tasks = [{ id: 1, done: false }]; let seen = null; const patchFn = async () => {}; return toggleTaskOptimistic({ tasks, taskId: 1, patchFn, onOptimisticUpdate: (t) => { seen = t; }, onRollback: () => {} }).then(() => expect(seen[0].done).toBe(true)); })()

tests.description: resolves with the optimistic array on success, without calling onRollback
tests.expr: (() => { const tasks = [{ id: 1, done: false }]; let rolledBack = false; const patchFn = async () => {}; return toggleTaskOptimistic({ tasks, taskId: 1, patchFn, onOptimisticUpdate: () => {}, onRollback: () => { rolledBack = true; } }).then((result) => { expect(rolledBack).toBe(false); return expect(result[0].done).toBe(true); }); })()

tests.description: calls onRollback with the original (unmodified) array on failure and re-throws
tests.expr: (() => { const tasks = [{ id: 1, done: false }]; let rolledBackTo = null; const patchFn = async () => { throw new Error('nope'); }; return toggleTaskOptimistic({ tasks, taskId: 1, patchFn, onOptimisticUpdate: () => {}, onRollback: (t) => { rolledBackTo = t; } }).then(() => { throw new Error('should have thrown'); }, (err) => { expect(err.message).toBe('nope'); return expect(rolledBackTo[0].done).toBe(false); }); })()

tests.description: does not mutate the original tasks array in place
tests.expr: (() => { const tasks = [{ id: 1, done: false }]; const patchFn = async () => {}; return toggleTaskOptimistic({ tasks, taskId: 1, patchFn, onOptimisticUpdate: () => {}, onRollback: () => {} }).then(() => expect(tasks[0].done).toBe(false)); })()

items.explanation: The function builds a new array (never mutating the original) with the target task's done flag flipped, shows it immediately via onOptimisticUpdate, then calls patchFn. On success it resolves with the optimistic array; on failure it calls onRollback with the untouched original array and re-throws so the caller still learns the write failed — exactly L3's toggleTaskOptimistic, node-verified on both the success and failure paths.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Snapshot — original tasks array, untouched
2️⃣ Optimistic — new array, flag flipped, shown immediately
3️⃣ On failure — onRollback(original), then re-throw

Why: this is L3's exact toggleTaskOptimistic — the re-throw is what keeps the rollback honest instead of silently hiding the failure.

tests.expr: (() => { const items = [{ id: 1, starred: false }]; const patchFn = async () => {}; return toggleStarOptimistic({ items, itemId: 1, patchFn, onOptimisticUpdate: () => {}, onRollback: () => {} }).then(() => expect(items[0].starred).toBe(false)); })()

items.explanation: The function builds a new array (never mutating the original) with the target item's starred flag flipped, shows it immediately via onOptimisticUpdate, then calls patchFn. On success it resolves with the optimistic array; on failure it calls onRollback with the untouched original array and re-throws so the caller still learns the write failed — the same pattern as toggleTaskOptimistic, applied to a different field.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Snapshot — original tasks array, untouched
2️⃣ Optimistic — new array, flag flipped, shown immediately
3️⃣ On failure — onRollback(original), then re-throw

Why: this is L3's exact toggleTaskOptimistic — the re-throw is what keeps the rollback honest instead of silently hiding the failure.

items.prompt: L3's extend-it question asks what happens if a task's "done" toggle and title edit are both in flight at once, and only the title edit fails. What's the risk with restoring "the snapshot from before this specific change"?
choices: There's no risk — snapshots always compose safely regardless of how many changes are in flight
If the done-toggle's optimistic change already landed before the title-edit rollback runs, restoring an older snapshot could accidentally revert the done-toggle too, even though it succeeded
Snapshots can only be taken once per session, so a second optimistic update would fail immediately
The done toggle and title edit can never both be in flight, so this scenario is impossible
items.explanation: A snapshot taken before the title edit doesn't know about the done-toggle that landed afterward — naively restoring it could wipe out an unrelated, successful change, which is why concurrent optimistic updates need more careful state tracking than a single before/after snapshot.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Toggle done — optimistic, in flight
2️⃣ Edit title — optimistic, in flight, then fails
❓ Rollback edit title — to which snapshot, given #1 may have already landed?

Why: this is the extend-it question from L3 — a single before/after snapshot is enough for one change at a time, but not obviously enough once changes overlap.

items.prompt: Why does the single-field boolean toggle in L3 count as "the simplest possible optimistic update," per the unit's own framing?
choices: Because there's exactly one prior value to remember and restore — more complex or concurrent changes complicate what "the snapshot" even means
Because boolean values never need rollback
Because it's the only kind of optimistic update that exists in practice
Because booleans are faster to send over the network than strings
items.explanation: A single boolean flip has one unambiguous prior value. The moment multiple fields or multiple concurrent updates are involved, "restore the snapshot" needs to account for other changes that may have landed in between — which is exactly what L3's extend-it question raises.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Toggle done — optimistic, in flight
2️⃣ Edit title — optimistic, in flight, then fails
❓ Rollback edit title — to which snapshot, given #1 may have already landed?

Why: this is the extend-it question from L3 — a single before/after snapshot is enough for one change at a time, but not obviously enough once changes overlap.

items.prompt: L3's failure-mode table warns about caching a GET response and never invalidating it after a related write. Why does this specifically matter once optimistic updates are involved?
choices: It doesn't — caching and optimistic updates are completely unrelated concerns
An optimistic write can update the UI's local state correctly while a separately cached GET response for the same data still holds the old, un-invalidated value
Optimistic updates automatically invalidate every cache in the application
Caching prevents optimistic updates from ever running
items.explanation: A toggled task's local state can be correct immediately from the optimistic update, while a cached list response for that same data (fetched through a different code path) has no way to know it should be considered stale — the two mechanisms need to actually agree on when data changes.
items.reference:
☑️ Optimistic toggle — this task's local state is correct now
💾 Cached list response — still holds the pre-toggle value, unless told otherwise

Why: caching and optimistic updates solve different problems, but a real app needs them to stay consistent with each other, not just each be individually correct.

items.prompt: What does L3's failure-mode table say is the risk of restoring rollback state by re-fetching instead of using a stored snapshot?
choices: A re-fetch after a failure can race with other changes made in the meantime, potentially reverting more than just the failed update
Re-fetching is always faster than using a snapshot, so there's no real risk
Re-fetching is impossible once an optimistic update has been applied
There's no risk — re-fetching and snapshotting are functionally identical
items.explanation: A snapshot captures the exact prior state at the moment the optimistic change began. A re-fetch instead asks the server for the current state, which may already reflect other changes made in between — reverting to it can undo more than just the one failed update.
items.reference:
☑️ Optimistic toggle — this task's local state is correct now
💾 Cached list response — still holds the pre-toggle value, unless told otherwise

Why: caching and optimistic updates solve different problems, but a real app needs them to stay consistent with each other, not just each be individually correct.

items.prompt: L3's `fetchTasksNaive` function always calls `fetcher()` directly with no memory of prior results. What's the direct consequence of that?
choices: Every call re-runs fetcher(), even when a previous call already retrieved the same data
The function automatically caches its result after the first call
The function only works the first time it's called
The function silently returns stale data without ever checking the server
items.explanation: With no cache, fetchTasksNaive has no way to know it already fetched this data before — every call hits the network again, regardless of whether anything changed.
items.reference:
🐢 fetchTasksNaive — always calls fetcher(), no memory
🐢 toggleTaskNaive — always awaits patchFn before returning anything

Why: these two naive functions are the concrete code-level version of the two problems L1/L2 describe in the abstract.

items.prompt: L3's `toggleTaskNaive` function awaits `patchFn` before returning anything to the caller. What's the direct consequence of that?
choices: The caller has nothing to show the user until the full server round trip completes — exactly the 800ms gap from the opening scenario
The function completes instantly regardless of server response time
The function automatically retries on failure
The function returns a cached value instead of contacting the server
items.explanation: Because the await blocks until patchFn resolves, the caller — and therefore the UI — has nothing to display until the server actually responds, reproducing the opening scenario's 800ms delay exactly.
items.reference:
🐢 fetchTasksNaive — always calls fetcher(), no memory
🐢 toggleTaskNaive — always awaits patchFn before returning anything

Why: these two naive functions are the concrete code-level version of the two problems L1/L2 describe in the abstract.

items.prompt: In L3's verified success path, `optimisticSeen[0].done` is already `true` before `patchFn` even resolves. What does this confirm?
choices: onOptimisticUpdate fires synchronously with the assumed new state, independent of when the server actually responds
patchFn is never actually called in the success case
The server responds instantly with no network delay
The optimistic value is only correct after the server confirms it
items.explanation: onOptimisticUpdate is called before patchFn is awaited — the caller sees the assumed new state immediately, which is the entire mechanism the unit is demonstrating.
items.reference:
✅ Success path — optimistic shown immediately, confirmed, no rollback
❌ Failure path — optimistic shown immediately, then rolled back + error thrown

Why: both paths start identically (show the optimistic state) — they only diverge once the server's actual response is known.

items.prompt: In L3's verified failure path, why does the code check `err.message === "Server rejected"` inside a catch block rather than just checking the rolled-back UI state?
choices: To confirm the original error is still propagated to the caller, not silently swallowed by the rollback logic
Because the UI state is never actually correct in the failure case
Because catching errors is optional and this check is redundant
To verify that patchFn was never called at all
items.explanation: The rolled-back UI state alone doesn't prove the caller learned about the failure — checking that the original error still reaches the caller confirms the `throw` inside `.catch` wasn't accidentally dropped.
items.reference:
